title: How Aphrodisiacs Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explain what aphrodisiacs are (distinguished from performance enhancers like Viagra), how sexual arousal works physiologically, the FDA's position that no compound is officially recognized as an aphrodisiac, and the role of testosterone. They cover historical and folk aphrodisiacs (Spanish fly, honey and the honeymoon, oysters, avocados, figs, animal genitalia), ginseng, chocolate and Montezuma, smell studies by Dr. Alan Hirsch (cheese pizza, buttered popcorn, lavender, pumpkin pie), pheromones and the twin-sister bar study, and the placebo effect. The episode closes with a blog plug and listener limericks.

entities.name: Smell and Taste Treatment and Research Center

segments.title: Opening banter and Spanish fly
segments.summary: Hosts open the show, then discuss Spanish fly, which is actually a beetle, and why it is dangerous and not an aphrodisiac.

segments.title: Definition of aphrodisiacs and sexual arousal
segments.summary: Aphrodisiac is defined as something that stimulates sexual desire, distinct from performance enhancers like Viagra. The hosts describe the physiology of arousal, including limbic system activation and blood flow to the genitals.

segments.title: FDA stance and testosterone
segments.summary: The FDA does not recognize any compound as an aphrodisiac because libido is hard to define and study. Testosterone affects arousal in men and women, citing a 2000 University of Utrecht study on sublingual testosterone.

segments.title: Historical aphrodisiacs: Persia, honeymoon, Rome
segments.summary: Ancient Persians believed honey was an aphrodisiac, and newlyweds drank honey for a month, giving rise to the word honeymoon. Ancient Rome was also big on aphrodisiacs.

segments.title: Food aphrodisiacs and resemblance theory
segments.summary: Oysters top aphrodisiac lists due to zinc and iron content. Foods resembling sex organs, such as avocados, figs, carrots, and bananas, were considered aphrodisiacs. Some cultures ate animal sex organs.

segments.title: Ginseng, chocolate, and Montezuma
segments.summary: Ginseng was reported to improve erectile function scores in a study. Chocolate contains phenylethylamine and serotonin, and Montezuma reportedly drank many goblets of chocolate daily.

segments.title: Smell, pheromones, and the twin study
segments.summary: Dr. Alan Hirsch's study measured penile blood flow in response to smells: cheese pizza, buttered popcorn, lavender, and pumpkin pie, with a black licorice and cucumber combination effective on women. Pheromones are discussed, including an informal bar study of twins where the one sprayed with pheromones got more attention.

segments.title: Placebo effect wrap-up
segments.summary: Hosts conclude that science does not support aphrodisiacs and that they may work as placebos.

segments.title: Blog plug and listener mail
segments.summary: Hosts promote the new stuff you should know blog on the website, then read listener limericks from Ryan in Victoria, British Columbia and Brendan Franklin in Tucson, Arizona.
